Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:68: Further, when occupied with Torah, one must be careful not to interrupt it with idle talk, for this is like mixing mundane with holy, and its punishment is severe, as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Shelach Lecha 162a): a heavenly voice declares in the Garden of Eden every day three things, before Betzalel opens with the mysteries of the wise, one of them being: whoever interrupts shall be cut off — meaning, whoever interrupts words of Torah for idle words, his life from this world shall be cut off, and his judgment stands in that world — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:69: This is what they say in the chapter Ein Dorshin (Chagigah 8b): Rabbi Levi said, whoever interrupts words of Torah and occupies himself with idle talk is fed coals of broom, as it is said, "who pluck saltwort with wormwood (siach), and roots of broom for their food" (Job 30:4). Rashi, peace be upon him, explains in Avodah Zarah, first chapter (3b), that this refers to one who interrupts for idle conversation (siach) — "malu'ach" (saltwort) meaning moist/idle words, and this is the essential meaning — another reading: written on tablets [luchot, playing on the word]. "Coals of broom" is explained in the preceding chapter in the name of Rashi, peace be upon him, regarding "sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of broom" (Psalms 120:4) — see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:70: The reason for this is that Torah is fire, and was given in fire, as it is said, "from His right hand went a fiery law for them" (Deuteronomy 33:2), and idle words are coals of fire, for speech comes from the fire of the heart; and when a person is occupied with Torah, his voice "hews out flames of fire" in holiness, but when occupied with idle talk, it is a foreign fire, and therefore "in his own net, which he has hidden, is he caught" — with the fire of blemish, fire shall consume him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:71: Regarding the reason for "whoever interrupts..." as stated, it is because Torah is your life and the length of your days — your life in this world, and length of days in the World to Come (see Tanchuma Shemini 11) — and therefore, measure for measure, he is punished in this world and in the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:72: When a person, while occupied with Torah, places the fear of the Holy One, blessed be He, before him, he will not come to interrupt, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, say in the Midrash on Eichah, on the verse, "pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord" (Lamentations 2:19), in these words: any Torah scholar who sits alone by himself and reads and studies, it is as though the Holy One, blessed be He, sits opposite him and reads and studies with him — therefore it says "before the presence of the Lord," and elsewhere it says, "and these encamped opposite those" (I Kings 20:29) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:73: And with this, this chapter is concluded — we have gathered the aspects of the particulars of speech that one must be careful of, to the extent our limited understanding allows, and whoever adds further such fences, the blessing of good shall come upon him:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:1: Now, having said in the preceding chapters that the matter of speech depends on the mouth, we wish to speak, connected to this matter, of the holiness of eating, which depends on the mouth — for King Solomon, peace be upon him, mentioned the guarding of the mouth in saying, "whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles" (Proverbs 21:23), and it is explained in Parashat Shemini (Zohar 41a-b), whose wording we quoted in chapter 11, that "his mouth" means the guarding of his mouth from impure foods. With God's help we shall explain the aspects of the holiness of eating regarding what is permitted, according to what is found in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, and in the words of the commentators.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:2: Just as our holy Torah mentioned the word "holiness" in [connection with] forbidden relations (Leviticus 20:7), and likewise in [connection with] tzitzit (Numbers 15:40) and in other places, as we explained at the beginning of this Gate, so it mentions it in the matter of foods; and therefore, at the end of Parashat Shemini, having mentioned the permitted and forbidden foods, it says there, "and you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy... and do not make your souls detestable" (Leviticus 11:44). It is explained in the Zohar regarding this that upon the impure foods, from which the Torah warns us, rests an external, impure spirit; therefore whoever eats of those things defiles his soul and shows about himself that he has no part in holiness or in the God of Israel, because the impure thing becomes a part of the limb within the person's essence, and the soul is clothed there — so he defiles his soul and defiles the soul clothed in the body. In this the wording of the Zohar is precise, saying, "whoever eats of those forbidden foods becomes attached to the Other Side and makes his soul and body abhorrent, and an impure spirit rests upon him" — and its saying "his soul and body" indicates what has been explained. They further elaborate on the punishment there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:3: Likewise one who eats his food for the sake of Heaven, as will be explained, and among the things the Torah permitted, upon which rests the spirit of righteousness of holiness and purity, the soul benefits from that eating from the side of the holiness within it — this is [the meaning of] "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" (Proverbs 13:25). According to the plain sense of the verse this is difficult, for what is "to the satisfaction of his soul" — since the soul is spiritual and holy and is not satisfied by this physical eating but only by the eating of Torah — and so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Beshalach 62b), that "the satisfaction of his soul" is the spiritual eating, which is the eating of Torah. In these words, it says there that a person should not eat until he has prayed for his sustenance, and they say, of blessed memory: Rabbi Yitzchak said, from here: "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — after satisfying his soul with prayer and reading Torah — so far his words. This shows he says "satisfaction of his soul" according to the true meaning, that is, the spiritual satisfaction pertaining to the soul; nevertheless, according to what we explained, that in the eating itself there is an aspect of holiness, the soul is satisfied from that very holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:4: Therefore it is fitting for a person to be stringent with himself regarding his own food, that it should have no aspect of prohibition at all — for the prophet Ezekiel praised himself for not eating of an animal that a sage had ruled on [permitting], even though it was permitted, once it fell into a doubt of prohibition, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, say in the chapter Eilu Treifot (Chullin 37b), on the verse, "neither came there abominable flesh into my mouth" (Ezekiel 4:14) — all the more so if there is an aspect of prohibition in the food itself, one should distance himself from it. There are indeed several matters where the later authorities disagree as to whose ruling is halachah, one forbidding and one permitting — and certainly the prophet Ezekiel, peace be upon him, would not have eaten such a thing, for the one who forbids it treats it as a piece of forbidden matter, which is more severe than [merely] a sage having ruled on it. And it is written in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Repentance, ch. 5) that the pious would separate from seventy gates of the gates of the permitted, out of fear of one gate of the gates of the forbidden.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:5: Similarly one must be careful in several other matters, not to buy things that carry a suspicion of prohibition except from a proper Jew who is precise about it as is fitting — for if he is suspect regarding it, he is not trusted, as we learn at the end of chapter 4 of Bechorot (mishnah 10): this is the general rule — whoever is suspect regarding a matter, one does not judge by his word nor accept his testimony. This applies particularly to bread, wine, meat, milk, cheese, and grape honey, and anything involving cooking by gentiles, except where permitted by explicit rulings of the halachic authorities.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:6: Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explain in Midrash Mishlei, on the verse (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul," several interpretations, all coming to one point, in these words: another interpretation, "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — this refers to Eliezer, Abraham's servant, who said to our mother Rebecca, "let me sip, please, a little water from your jar" (Genesis 24:17) — a single sip. "But the belly of the wicked shall want" — this refers to the wicked Esau, who said to our father Jacob, "let me gulp down, please, some of that red, red stuff" (Genesis 25:30) — that wicked one opened his mouth wide like a camel and said, "open my mouth and I will keep going," pouring the whole pot into it, as we learn (Shabbat 24:3), "one does not stuff a camel or force-feed it, but one may pour food into its mouth."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:7: Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — this refers to Ruth the Moabite, as it is written, "and she ate, and was satisfied, and left [some]" (Ruth 2:14). Rabbi Yitzchak said, you learn two things from this: either blessing dwelt in that righteous man's [Boaz's] hand, or blessing dwelt in the belly of that righteous woman — from the fact that it is written "and she ate, and was satisfied, and left," it appears that blessing dwelt in the belly of that righteous woman. "But the belly of the wicked shall want" — these are the nations of the world, idol worshipers, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:8: Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — this refers to Hezekiah king of Judah. They said of Hezekiah king of Judah that he would eat two bundles of vegetables, and one litra of meat was brought before him each day, and Israel would slander him and say, "This is a king? Retzin was a king! Delight and kingship are fitting for Retzin son of Remaliah!" This is what is written, "because this people has refused the waters of Shiloach that flow gently" (Isaiah 8:6) — this refers to Hezekiah king of Judah, who purified Israel with a mikveh of forty se'ah, equal to the numerical value of "le'at" (gently). The Holy One, blessed be He, said, "You bring up food and are satisfied, therefore behold, the Lord brings up over you the waters of the river." "But the belly of the wicked shall want" — this refers to Mesha king of Moab, who was a sheep-herder — what is "noked"? A shepherd, as it is said, "and Mesha king of Moab was a sheep-herder" (II Kings 3:4). And in Yalkut (Mishlei, remez 950) they bring it in another manner: "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — this is Hezekiah, as stated; "but the belly of the wicked shall want" — this is Pekah son of Remaliah, who would eat three hundred fledglings as dessert after a meal — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:9: Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — these are the kings of Israel and the house of David. "But the belly of the wicked shall want" — these are the eastern kings, for whom a hundred sheep would be brought up for each and every one. Another interpretation, "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — this is the Holy One, blessed be He, who said to Israel, "My children, of all the offerings you bring before Me, do I derive any benefit from them except the pleasing scent?" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:10: This passage shows the greatness of the righteous, who content themselves with little, and the wicked, who are not satisfied with little, the reason being that their belly is deficient, so that the whole world would not suffice to fill their belly, and it always appears to them that their belly is not full.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:11: When a person sees that everything he adds to his eating adds flesh for the worm — for this is his end — certainly it is fitting to distance himself from excessive eating, particularly except on Sabbaths and festivals, for one who indulges in eating and drinking on the six weekdays more than needed for the sustenance of his soul and body is punished; concerning them it is said, "and I will spread dung upon your faces, even the dung of your festivals" (Malachi 2:3). This verse is explained in tractate Shabbat (151b): Rav Huna said, this refers to those who neglect words of Torah and make all their days like festivals. And it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel 199b), whose wording we quoted in the Gate of Awe, chapter 12, that after three days his belly bursts, and they cast the dung upon his face and say to him, "Take what you chose, and made all your days like festivals and holy times" — see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:12: Further, they say in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah 141a), in these words: the bodies of the righteous, who were not drawn in this world after the pleasures of that strong kelipah, the spirit of impurity does not rule over them at all — for they had no part with it whatsoever in this world, following after that strong kelipah and its pleasures and delights, and its preparations; so it becomes defiled after the soul departs from it. The bodies of the righteous, who take delight in this world only in the pleasures of a mitzvah and the meals of Sabbaths, festivals, and holy times — that impure spirit cannot rule over them, for they took no pleasure at all from its own [side]; since they took nothing of its own, it has no permission over them at all; fortunate is he who does not benefit at all from its own [side] — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:13: This makes clear that whoever indulges in feasts that are not for Sabbaths and festivals indulges from the kelipah, and the kelipah rules over him at his death. This kelipah is the hard shell of the nut, which is the second shell, and therefore it is called the "strong kelipah," as explained above, that the first shell of the nut is soft.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:14: The reason that indulgences are in this harder kelipah is that everything a person eats beyond the sustenance of the soul is indulgence, and he adds flesh to his body for the worm; and the reason is that according to how much one is drawn after the worm, which is the kelipah, the kelipah will rule over him — for the flesh of a person's body is drawn from the skin of the serpent, as is explained in the Tikkunim (42), in these words: at the time Pharaoh's daughter touched him [Moses in the basket], the Shechinah flew from him, and therefore, when he wished to draw near to her at the burning bush, it said to him, "do not come closer," until he stripped off that body which Pharaoh's daughter had touched — there it was shown to him that a person's body in this world is the tzara'at from the skin of the serpent; afterward, once stripped of it and having returned to the Garden of Eden, he is clothed in his own holy body — this is [the meaning of] "and behold, it returned like his flesh" (Exodus 4:7) — so far his words, as pertains to us. There is no entry for the outsider to cause one to sin except from the side of food — for Samael and his classes are spiritual, and man is physical, and they have no entry point or affinity to attach to him; but when a person is drawn after his desire, he gives a part to his flesh, which was made from a putrid drop that is from the kelipah, and thereby he is caused to sin. As is said in the Tikkunim (53b), all sins are from the limbs of the putrid drop, and they say there that the putrid drop is an evil handmaid — and therefore it is said in the Sifrei (Ha'azinu, piska 13), as we shall quote below, that a person rebels only through eating and drinking.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:15: Further, they say, of blessed memory, in Berachot (29b): Elijah said to Rav Yehudah, Rav Sala's brother, "Do not be angry and you will not sin; do not get drunk and you will not sin." Rabbeinu Yonah's students explain "do not get drunk and you will not sin" to mean: do not eat to satiation, so as not to come to sin — for when a person is satiated and drawn after his pleasures, he forgets matters of the Creator, exalted be He. Rashi, of blessed memory, explains "do not get drunk" as literally not becoming intoxicated with wine, and this is correct, since the Targum renders "and he drank of the wine, and was drunk" (Genesis 9:21) as "and he drank of wine and became intoxicated"; and likewise "a drunkard of wine" is rendered "intoxicated with wine." However, one can also reconcile the students of Rabbeinu Yonah's explanation, since ordinarily a person does not become intoxicated except through much eating when he is satiated — and by this both explanations are correct.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:16: Further, it says in Bereshit Rabbah (38:7), regarding the generation of the dispersion, in these words: Rav Chelbo said, wherever you find contentment of spirit, Satan accuses; Rabbi Levi said, wherever you find eating and drinking, Satan accuses — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:17: In the Midrash HaNe'elam (Zohar Parashat Chayei Sarah 127a), regarding the resurrection of the dead, on the matter of "and take a wife for my son from there" (Genesis 24:4), Rabbi Yitzchak said: that body which suffered with me in that world, and had no pleasure and pined away because of fear of its Maker — that body you shall take for Isaac — so far his words, as pertains to us. From this it appears explicitly that whoever suffers and distances himself from pleasures fears the Lord, as it says "because of fear of its Maker" — the intent being that he does not wish to enjoy so as not to come to sin, for pleasure brings one to sin, as we have explained and shall further explain, please God. See, see how much one must distance oneself from the kelipah of pleasures and subdue it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:18: At the end of the passage it says, "fortunate is he who does not benefit at all from its own [side]" — he varies his wording, for above he said "who does not take delight from its own [side]" and here he says "who does not benefit from its own [side]." The intent is to tell us that there is an additional greatness for one who does not even have a small benefit from the kelipah, all the more so pleasure — and this is the nature of the phrase "zakai ihu" ("fortunate is he"), meaning an additional greatness. This is the way my teacher, peace be upon him, would explain it: wherever the Zohar says "zakai ihu," it indicates something more praiseworthy than what preceded.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:19: It is explained that "not having benefit" refers to contenting oneself with a small amount for the sustenance of the soul — this being the sustenance of a Torah scholar, which Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains (Parashat Beshalach 62a), whose wording we quoted above: fortunate is the portion of the body that can be sustained on the sustenance of the soul. It seems to me that the intent is that this kelipah — the kelipah of the worm — should not rule over him; therefore a person should distance himself from this harsh kelipah, which is what causes a person to pursue eating and drinking.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:20: Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, author of Menorat HaMa'or, writes (part 2, letter 17), in these words: because of the lowliness of his name, the wicked person who pursues eating and drinking is called "Oy Lo" ("woe to him") — an acrostic of "eat and drink," for it is said to you (Proverbs 23:7) — for he thinks this world was created only for eating and drinking; and those who pursue their desire, today they satiate themselves with the permitted, and tomorrow with the forbidden, and when they cannot obtain it from their own, they rob from others. Concerning this the Torah commanded regarding the "rebellious and stubborn son," who is to be killed if his father saw that he ate two portions of meat and half a log of Italian wine — for since he has begun pursuing pleasures, he will come to consume his father's property, and if he cannot find it, he will come to rob people; and it is better that he die innocent than die guilty. So they say in the chapter Ben Sorer U'Moreh (Sanhedrin 72a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:21: Therefore one must be careful not to pursue excesses, for excessive eating is what brings a person to sin, and immediately his inclination becomes arrogant over him, as they say in the Sifrei (Ha'azinu, piska 13), in these words: "but Jeshurun grew fat and kicked" (Deuteronomy 32:15) — because of satiety they rebel. And so you find with the generation of the flood, who rebelled before the Omnipresent only because of eating, drinking, and tranquility — what is said of them? "And the whole earth was of one language" (Genesis 11:1) [indicating unity and prosperity that led to arrogance]. And so we find with the men of the tower [of Babel], who rebelled before the Omnipresent, and so on; and so it says, "as I live, says the Lord, Sodom your sister has not done, she nor her daughters, as you have done" (Ezekiel 16:48). You find with the people of the generation of the desert that they rebelled before the Omnipresent only because of eating, as it is said, "and the people sat down to eat and to drink" (Exodus 32:6) — what is said of them? "They have turned aside quickly out of the way" (Exodus 32:8). The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, tell Israel: when you enter the land, you are destined to rebel against Me only because of eating and drinking, as it is said, "for when I shall have brought them into the land which I swore to their fathers, flowing with milk and honey, and they shall eat and be satisfied, and grow fat, and turn to other gods" (Deuteronomy 31:20). Moses said to Israel: when you enter the land, you are destined to rebel only because of eating and drinking, as it is said, "lest you eat and be satisfied, and build good houses..." (Deuteronomy 8:12-13) "and your herds and flocks multiply" — what is said of them? "Then your heart shall be lifted up, and you shall forget the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 8:14). And so you find with Job's sons and daughters, that calamity came upon them only because of eating, drinking, and tranquility, as it is said, "while he was yet speaking, another came and said, your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine... and behold, a great wind..." (Job 1:18-19). And so you find with the Ten Tribes, that they were exiled only because of eating, drinking, and tranquility, as it is said, "who lie upon beds of ivory... who drink wine in bowls... therefore now shall they go into captivity at the head of those who go captive" (Amos 6:4-6-7) — and they further elaborate there — so far his words, as pertains to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:22: In the Tosefta of Sotah, chapter 3 (item 3), they prove all this from the verses regarding the men of the tower [of Babel], as it is said, "and it came to pass, as they journeyed from the east, they found a valley in the land of Shinar, and they dwelt there" (Genesis 11:2) — and "dwelling" (yeshivah) refers only to eating and drinking, as it is said, "and the people sat down (vayeshev) to eat and to drink" (Exodus 32:6) — this caused them, "and they said..." and so on. The men of Sodom became arrogant before the Omnipresent only because of the good He had bestowed on them, as it is said, "the earth, out of which comes bread... a place whose stones are sapphires... a path no bird of prey has known" (Job 28:5-7). The men of Sodom said, "Since food comes out of our land, and silver and gold come out of our land, and precious stones and pearls come out of our land, we have no need for people to come to us except to diminish us — let us arise and abolish the foot-traveler [the practice of hospitality] from among us." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, "When I did good for you, you seek to abolish the foot-traveler from among you — I will abolish the foot [of your existence] from among you and forget you from the world." What does it say? "He breaks open a channel away from where people dwell... the tents of robbers prosper" (Job 12:5-6), and so it says, "as I live, says the Lord, Sodom your sister has not done — behold, this was the iniquity of Sodom your sister, pride, fullness of bread..." (Ezekiel 16:48-49) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:23: Just as one must be careful of excessive eating, so one must be careful of excessive wine, for a small amount of it benefits the digestion and sharpens the mind, as they say, of blessed memory (Horayot 13b), "wine and spices make one sharp-minded" — but one who becomes drunk from it harms his body, destroys his intellect, and causes himself all the evils of the world, as we find with Noah, who brought upon himself evil and disgrace and caused himself to curse his own descendant, as we learn in Sanhedrin (70a): a Galilean preacher expounded — thirteen "vavs" ("and"s) are said regarding wine: "and Noah began (vayachel) to be a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard; and he drank of the wine, and was drunk; and he was uncovered; and Ham saw; and he told his two brothers... and Shem and Japheth took... and laid it on both their shoulders... and they went... and they covered... and Noah awoke from his wine, and knew what his youngest son had done to him..." — so far his words. It seems to me that the intent of these thirteen "vavs" is that they all contain "vav-yod" to indicate "oy vay" (woe, woe), and they are thirteen to indicate a blemish in unity, since "echad" (one/unity) numerically equals thirteen; further, thirteen times six equals seventy-eight, equal to the count of the three Names in "the Lord reigns, the Lord has reigned..." There is necessary confirmation for this from what it says further there: the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Noah, "You should have learned from Adam, whom only wine caused [to sin]," as they say in the Midrash — that tree from which Adam ate was a vine, for there is nothing that brings wailing into the world upon a person like wine — so far his words. This shows that Adam's sin was involved [with wine], and they say, of blessed memory, that a trace of disqualification was cast into Adam through that sin. And it says, "there is nothing that brings wailing," being precise about the term "vav" (associated with "vay," woe).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:24: Further, we say there in tractate Eruvin (65a): Rabbi Chanan said, wine was created in this world only to comfort mourners and to pay the reward of the wicked [in this world, to their detriment in the World to Come], as it is said, "give strong drink to him who is perishing, and wine to those of bitter soul" (Proverbs 31:6). Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi] said, what is [the meaning of] "do not look upon the wine when it is red, when it gives its color in the cup" (Proverbs 23:31)? Do not look at wine, which reddens the faces of the wicked in this world, [but] ultimately whitens their faces [with shame] in the World to Come. Rava said, "do not look upon the wine when it is red," for its end is blood. Rav Kahana raised a contradiction: it is written "yisham" ("it destroys") but read "yisamach" ("it gladdens") — if he merits, it gladdens him; if he does not merit, it destroys him — and this is what Rava meant, "wine and spices make one sharp-minded" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:25: Further, they say in Midrash Mishlei, on the verse (Proverbs 23:29), "who has woe, who has sorrow": Rabbi Simon said, come and see how harsh wine is, for thirteen "vavs" were said regarding wine at the outset, and so on, as expounded. It further says: Solomon came and explained, with his wisdom, "who has woe, who has sorrow" — this refers to one who becomes drunk — woe to him and to his father, as it is said, "if a man has a rebellious and stubborn son" (Deuteronomy 21:18). "Who has strife" — because when he becomes drunk with his wine he reveals secrets between one person and another, and he sows discord. "Who has complaint" — because when he becomes drunk with his wine he utters excessive complaints, and so on. "Who has wounds without cause" — because when he becomes drunk with his wine he goes and causes a wound and a bruise. Why "without cause"? Because he has no [proper] judgment [reason for it]. "Who has redness of eyes" — [this refers to one] who drinks according to his need, this being what is written, "his eyes shall be red with wine, and his teeth white with milk" (Genesis 49:12); Rabbi Yirmiyah said, do not read "lavan shinayim" (white of teeth) but "levaven shinayim" ("gladden the elderly") — just as milk satisfies the mind of an infant, so wine restores the mind of an elder.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:26: What is written after it (Proverbs 23:30)? "Those who tarry long over wine, those who go to seek out mixed wine." Rabbi Elazar said, woe to one who neglects words of Torah and rises early for wine. What is written after it? "Do not look upon the wine when it is red, when it gives its color (eino) in the cup (bakos)." Rabbi Yochanan said, it is written "bakis" (in the purse) but we read "bakos" (in the cup) — why is this? A buyer sets his eye on the cup, but a seller sets his eye on the purse. And in Vayikra Rabbah (12:1) it explains the completion of the verse explicitly: "it goes down smoothly (yithalech bemesharim)" — in the end he turns his house into a level field (mishor) — from that copper pot [he had, he goes down] to an earthenware pot, [and eventually] a servant sells it and drinks wine with its price — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:27: What is written after it (Proverbs 23:32)? "At the last it bites like a serpent, and stings like an adder." Just as the serpent bites and kills, and separates between death and life, so wine separates between death and life — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:28: Further, they say, "lest he drink, and forget the decreed law (mechukak)" (Proverbs 31:5) — "mechukak" numerically equals 248 — meaning, through drinking wine, he will forget to fulfill the 248 positive commandments. In these words: "lest he drink, and forget mechukak" — whoever drinks much wine will eventually forget the 248 limbs within him — this is [the meaning of] "lest he drink, and forget mechukak," written [in a form suggesting] "from" "chukak," these being the 248 [limbs]. Rabbi Chanina bar Papa said, the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "I had a great house, and I destroyed it only because of wine." And the Rabbis say, "I had two princes, and they died only because of wine," as Rabbi Yishmael taught, the two sons of Aaron died only because they entered [the Sanctuary] having drunk wine — so far his words. "He should drink and forget the decreed law" — Rabbi Shimon said, these are the words of Torah, which are decreed, and it is written among them, "you shall not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:13). It further says, he will forget the Torah, which was given through the Lawgiver (mechokek), namely Moses, as it is said, "for there was the portion of the lawgiver (mechokek), reserved" (Deuteronomy 33:21) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:29: Further, in Midrash Rabbah, Parashat Nazir (Bamidbar Rabbah 10:2), in these words: "do not look upon the wine when it is red" (Proverbs 23:31) — the holy spirit warned regarding wine, that a person should not become drunk. Why? "When it is red" — for its end is blood, [meaning] that he transgresses a sin for which he becomes liable to death. Another interpretation: for he desires the blood of niddah and the blood of zivah. "When it gives its color (eino) in the cup (kos)" — written "kis" (purse) — through the cup he sets his eye on the purse [in some interpretation, or elsewhere reversed] — the Torah spoke in clean language, meaning that he will come upon forbidden relations. "It goes down smoothly" — in the end his wife says, "I saw it as a red rose," and he does not separate [from her during her impurity]. Rabbi Assi said, if he is a Torah scholar, he eventually declares the impure pure and the pure impure. Another interpretation, "it goes down smoothly" — in the end he permits transgressions and makes them free as an open field, converses with a woman in the marketplace, speaks vulgarly in his drunkenness, and is not ashamed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:30: "At the last it bites like a serpent" — just as, through the serpent enticing Eve to drink wine, the earth was cursed because of it, as it is said, "cursed is the ground because of you" (Genesis 3:17), so, through wine, a third of the world was cursed, as it is said, "and Noah awoke from his wine..." "cursed be Canaan" (Genesis 9:24-25) — this was Ham, who was his third son and called "the father of Canaan," and so they cursed him. Just as an adder separates between death and life, so wine separates a person from the ways of life to the ways of death, because wine causes him to fall into idolatry — this being what is written, "your eyes shall behold strange things" (Proverbs 23:33), as it is written, "there shall be no strange god among you" (Psalms 81:10). Another interpretation: he comes upon a married woman, as it says, "and why should you go astray, my son, with a strange woman" (Proverbs 5:20) — so far. From this passage you learn that wine causes idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:31: Further there, another interpretation: that he treats the commandments as strange, as it is said, "proud, haughty, mocker (letz) is his name, dealing in wrathful pride" (Proverbs 21:24) — this refers to the drunkard, who is called haughty and mocker. From where "haughty"? As it is said, "and moreover, wine deals treacherously with the haughty man, and he does not rest" (Habakkuk 2:5). From where "mocker"? As it is written, "wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler; whoever is deceived thereby is not wise" (Proverbs 20:1) — so he is called "mocker" as well; and you already know that the class of mockers does not receive the presence of the Shechinah (Sanhedrin 103a). Further there, "and your heart shall utter perverse things" (Proverbs 23:33) — that he turns his face away from the Holy One, blessed be He, and from the commandments, as it says, "for they are a generation of perverse things" (Deuteronomy 32:20).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:32: "And you shall be as one who lies in the midst of the sea" (Proverbs 23:34) — this refers to Noah, who lay in the ark twelve months amid the waters of the flood, and because he drank and became drunk, a defect occurred to him, that he became emasculated. "As one who lies upon the top of a mast" — this refers to the primordial Adam, who is the head of all human beings, upon whom, because of wine, death was decreed, causing him to bring the pangs of death into the world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:33: "They have struck me, and I was not sick" (Proverbs 23:35) — woe to the adulterer who does not learn a lesson from what has happened to him! He saw what happened to the sotah (suspected adulteress) because of wine, and did not learn a lesson. "They have beaten me, and I did not know it" — he saw in the Torah what happened to the adulterer because of wine, and did not know how to understand — rather he said, "when shall I awake yet again?" — for as long as he has the leisure to occupy himself with licentiousness, he will pursue it. Thus we learn that wine causes licentiousness, and therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, wrote in the Torah the portion of the Nazirite after the portion of the sotah — so that a person not act like the adulterer and adulteress who drank wine and were corrupted, but rather one who fears sin should make himself a Nazirite from wine — therefore it is said, "if a man or woman shall separate himself..." (Numbers 6:2) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:34: What we find in the Gemara — "wine and spices make one sharp-minded" — refers to a small amount of wine, well diluted; but undiluted wine is what is harmful, and this too is understood there in the Midrash Bamidbar Rabbah — see there — but we shall not quote its wording so as not to be lengthy.
